page_placements.theme: Capacity limits and computation in superposition (theory and constructions)

record.tranche_reason: Experimentally tests a circuits-in-superposition construction using hand-coded toy networks. It bears on the capacity-pressure mechanism in V3, but does not measure polysemantic responses in trained networks.
record.gate_note: The study measures how accurately a toy MLP carries out multiple conditional circuits embedded in superposition. It does not inspect individual neurons' responses to input features. The discussion of GPT-2 and other work is speculation or cited work, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study hand-codes ReLU MLPs that embed many conditional rotation circuits in superposition, then measures circuit readout errors. Superposition is built in by construction, not observed arising in a network. No neuron's response selectivity is measured, so the study cannot show whether neurons are polysemantic or why. Its results concern the noise cost of computing in superposition, a related but different construct from polysemantic neurons. So it tests no version, including V3. The GPT-2 remarks are speculation or early unpublished observations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say the construction 'seems to work' but only a limited number of independent circuits fit before errors compound and explode. Errors grow superlinearly with depth and with z because noise switches on ReLUs that should stay off. They speculate that real models exploit shared structure, and may have few more independent circuits than neurons. An author comment notes the framework works for T(d/D)^2 < 0.004.
record.recipe_differences: Hand-coded ReLU MLPs embed conditional rotation circuits and evaluate circuit-readout errors. This is not a neuron-response or feature-interpretation procedure from the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Errors vary with depth, number of simultaneously active circuits z, and T(d/D)^2; the text says larger values tend to increase errors and make predictions worse.

fits_no_version.finding: In hand-coded ReLU MLPs (D=1000, T=557, d=4), computing many independent circuits in superposition accumulates noise with depth and active-circuit count. Inactive circuits switch on and cause cascading 'seizures'. Only about T≈2D/d circuits fit stably for a few layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Computation (not just storage) in superposition is capacity-limited: independent circuits beyond roughly the neuron count incur compounding interference noise.

record.problems: The experiments use hand-coded toy networks rather than trained models and do not measure individual-neuron response selectivity. Many numerical results are presented only in figures; the text cautions that some worst-case points still fluctuate with sample size. The authors also note that the error calculations rely on assumptions that fail when noise becomes large.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every plotted layer, network size, or active-circuit count: Figures 5–11 present many values only graphically, and the text reports the aggregate trends and the specific contrasts retained above. Cited results and speculation about language-model memorization were excluded.

untested.parts: No language model neurons are measured.
Does not test whether trained networks' polysemantic neurons arise from superposition. Superposition is hand-imposed and neuron responses are not inspected.
No initialization, regularization or training-noise effects; no training at all.
No comparison of architectures or activation functions.
No comparison of measurement or scoring procedures.

record.verdict_notes: Hand-coded, untrained toy construction; the rows measure the authors' own method's error, not polysemantic neurons. The reader's V3 links and labels are dropped. Lucius's GPT-2 decomposition remark is an informal early observation, not a reported result.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or vision-neuron responses are measured.
No language model neurons or token/context responses are measured.

Tests a hand-coded toy construction for representing and computing multiple circuits in superposition, not whether trained networks spontaneously develop polysemantic neurons, or whether superposition causes their mixed responses.
No initialization, regularization, or training-noise effects are tested.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularization effects on polysemantic neuron prevalence or performance is made.
No neuron explanations or shared-feature hypotheses are evaluated.
No comparison of neuron-measurement or explanation-scoring procedures is made.

relation.reason: Superposition is assumed by construction; the study does not test whether it makes neurons polysemantic. The reader's 'tests' is wrong.

tranche.reason: Hand-coded superposition circuits test the authors' own construction. No neuron polysemanticity or selectivity is measured, and superposition is built in. The reader's T2 is wrong.

source_check.notes: All values are figure-only and stated only in words. Figures 4-7 show the single D=1000, T=557 network, while Figures 8-11 show the D/T sweep (R6/R7 subjects need fixing). The T(d/D)^2<0.004 regime comes from an author comment. The text says MSE grows superlinearly with depth, not with z, so the pack's authors_conclusion overstates on z. The post never mentions polysemanticity.

statements.correction: With d=4 and D=1000 (T=557 used; 2D/d=500), fitting about 2D/d circuits was already hard. Noise stayed small enough only in the first few layers. Readout errors grow with depth (mean squared error grows superlinearly) and with z. At z=1, all 557 circuits beat the baseline only for the first two rotations, and at z=3 some circuit fails at the first rotation. As errors grow, they switch on neurons that active circuits do not use ('seizure'), starting with inactive circuits' On-indicators. The authors find many more independent circuits very difficult to fit, and think more active error correction could stabilize more layers.
statements.problem: D=1000, T=557 and d=4 are right, as is the claim that noise grows with depth and with the number of active circuits. 'Only about T of 2D/d circuits fit stably' is garbled and overstates the result: even at T≈2D/d, noise stayed small enough only in the first few layers. The text also says neurons that active circuits do not use switch on, starting with the inactive On-indicators. It does not say that whole inactive circuits switch on.
